newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK residential prices seen continuing rise - M.Stanley.
newsitem.headline: HK residential prices seen continuing rise - M.Stanley.

text.p: The threat of government intervention to reduce property speculation should cap price rises in the Hong Kong real estate market at about 20 percent, Morgan Stanley Asia strategist Peter Churchouse said on Friday.
"With the threat of intervention, or actual intervention, they will be down to the 15 to 20 percent level (one year from now)," he told a meeting of the American Chamber of Commerce.
He said he thought the goverment would be successful in curbing speculative excesses without causing a crash.
"I think if the market was left unfettered that (the rise) could be 60 or 70 percent easily," he said.

Demand for housing would remain strong, fed by stable interest rates in the United States and Hong Kong, competition among banks for mortgage business, low unemployment of 2.5 percent, rising household incomes of eight to 12 percent per year and a good affordability picture, Churchouse said.
Natural population growth of about 50,000 per year in the colony and another 50,000 to 55,000 a year coming from mainland China should help keep demand for housing high, said Churchouse.
"That is going to produce in an absolute sense a very strong upward surge in demand for housing of one kind or another," he said.
The British colony reverts to Chinese sovereignty at midnight on June 30.
Housing supply should remain tight, with 26,000-27,000 units available in 1997, well below the long-term average of 30,000-32,000 units in the late 1980s, he said.
Supply should increase in 1998 to 33,000-35,000 units, still modest amounts in terms of the demand conditions, he said.

"Essentially, over the next two years, we're not expecting to see anything like an oversupply situation building up in the private residential market at all," said Churchouse. "In fact if anything, it's going to be a tight market, not a loose market."
Based on the strength of the economy and housing price growth of 15-20 percent, property stocks should outperform the Hang Seng Index over the next year by about five percent, he said.
Churchouse was bullish on the blue-chip index, saying that based on historical cycles it should hit 26,000 to 28,000 points by mid-1999 before correcting by about 40 percent.
The index closed at 13,113.26 points on Friday.

He also said he expected the upturn in the office rentals market, which began in mid-1996, to continue over the next 12 to 18 months. Vacancy rates should be lower than the seven to 9.5 percent that Morgan Stanley had previously thought, he said.
Consumers, legislators and business lobbies have voiced concern about the rapid rise in residential property prices, which climbed some 20-30 percent in 1996.

Last month, the government said it welcomed voluntary moves by developers to curb rampant property speculation. But it warned that it would have to impose tougher measures if voluntary moves proved insufficient.
The focus of concern has been in the luxury sector, where prices jumped 30-40 percent last year.
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority recommended in January that banks limit mortgage lending for purchases of luxury properties.
Churchouse said that since luxury homes amounted to only 2.3 percent of the property sector, any future government intervention would be better aimed at the rest of the market.
